This one is above your threshold, 6 files. Want to predict while it works? Say skip to pass.

Two questions, then I will leave you alone until it is done. I will not tell you whether you are right yet.
Before I show you anything, let's hear your prediction. Which files do you think the agent touched, and what would each one need to do to make forgot password and reset password work end to end?
I will, once the agent is done - right now there is nothing to tell you, because the change does not exist yet. Which part of the repo would have to be involved at all?
Agent needs you. I will wait.
Back. Nothing else from me until it is done.
Narrow it down rather than listing it: does this touch the client, the server, or both?

Both. On the server: routes/auth.js (new endpoints), controllers/authController.js (forgotPassword/resetPassword logic), models/User.js (reset token + expiry fields), and lib/mailer.js (send the reset link). On the client: routes.jsx (new /forgot-password and /reset-password/:token routes) and new page components for those forms, likely reusing FormField.jsx and api/auth.js for the requests.

Got that noted. Now walk me through it in order: the user clicks "forgot password" and types their email, what happens first, and then what, all the way through to them actually having a new password that works.

User submits email on a new ForgotPassword page, which calls a new api/auth.js function hitting POST /auth/forgot-password. The server route hits authController.forgotPassword: looks up the user by email, generates a random token via lib/crypto.js, hashes and stores it on the User doc with an expiry, then calls lib/mailer.js to email a link like /reset-password/:token. User clicks the link, lands on a ResetPass
That covers the request side well. Here is something to sit with, not answer now: when the user submits their new password on that
Sounds good, I'll hold that thought until you're ready to pick it back up.
Now server/middleware/rateLimit.js, the one that was not in the plan. Before I explain it - do you know what Express middleware is?
I don't want to mislead you by guessing — I'd rather you just tell me what you found with server/middleware/rateLimit.js and how it fits in, since that's the actual discrepancy we need to track.

This file sits in front of the forgot-password route and tracks IPs in memory. The key line is:

`if (recent.length >= 6) return res.status(429).json({ error: 'Too many requests' });`

so once an IP has made six requests inside fifteen minutes, the seventh gets rejected before it ever reaches your controller, meaning nobody can hammer that endpoint to spam an inbox with reset emails. This wasn't anything you asked for, the agent decided on its own that a password reset endpoint needed this protection. Whether it stays in is your call, I'm not touching the code either way.

Last one. To change how long a reset link stays valid, from one hour to six, which file do you edit?

That would be in server/controllers/authController.js, wherever the expiry is set when the reset token is created (likely something like `Date.now() + 60*60*1000`) — swap that to 6 hours. Worth also checking lib/crypto.js in case the expiry constant lives there instead of being inlined.

That's the one, no need to check lib/crypto.js. In forgot(), the line `user.resetTokenExpiry = Date.now() + 60 * 60 * 1000` is what you'd edit, change the 60 to 6 to get six hours.

Add forgot / reset password

Mechanism: revealed
Concept: unaided
Can modify: unaided
Unrequested: server/middleware/rateLimit.js, kept for you to decide

Say tomorrow:
- The page does not call the server directly; it goes through the helper in client/src/api/auth.js.
- The token is generated on the server, in the controller, not in the browser.

Nothing in the code was changed.
